name: Lavoisier and Combustion
statement: By weighing what he burned, Lavoisier showed burning is combining with oxygen and that mass is conserved.
meaning: Lavoisier and combustion refers to the experiments and theory of the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier in the 1770s and 1780s, which explained what happens when things burn and, in doing so, launched the chemical revolution. Before Lavoisier, combustion was explained by the phlogiston theory, which held that burning substances released a fire-substance called phlogiston into the air. By carefully weighing substances before and after they burned or were heated, often in sealed vessels, Lavoisier showed instead that combustion is a chemical process in which a burning substance combines with a component of the air, which he named oxygen. He demonstrated, for example, that metals gain rather than lose weight when heated in air, because they take up oxygen, contradicting the phlogiston theory's prediction. His quantitative approach also established the law of conservation of mass: in a chemical reaction, matter is neither created nor destroyed, so the total mass stays the same. Lavoisier named oxygen and recognized hydrogen as an element, and set out his new chemistry in his 1789 Elementary Treatise on Chemistry. Widely called the father of modern chemistry, he transformed the subject into a quantitative science, though oxygen itself was independently isolated by Priestley and Scheele.
mechanism: Lavoisier's central method was quantitative: he weighed everything precisely, before and after a reaction, often working in closed vessels so that no matter could escape or enter unnoticed. When a substance burns, the phlogiston theory predicted it should lose weight as phlogiston escaped, but Lavoisier found that metals heated in air actually gain weight. He explained this by proposing that the metal combines with a part of the air, forming a calx, or oxide, that weighs more than the original metal by exactly the weight of air absorbed. In a decisive experiment he heated mercury in a closed volume of air until it formed a red calx, noting that a portion of the air was consumed; on then strongly heating the calx, he recovered the mercury and released a gas equal in amount to the air that had disappeared, and this gas supported combustion and respiration vigorously. He named it oxygen. Combustion, respiration, and the rusting of metals were thus all seen as the same kind of process: chemical combination with oxygen. Because he accounted for the weights of all the gases involved, not just the solids, his experiments also showed that the total mass of the substances is unchanged by the reaction, establishing the conservation of mass and making chemistry a precise, balance-sheet science.

examples.text: Lavoisier showed a metal heated in air gains weight by combining with oxygen, contradicting the phlogiston theory's prediction of loss.
Heating mercury consumed part of the air to form a calx, and reheating the calx released the same amount of gas, which he named oxygen.
By weighing all reactants and products, including gases, he showed the total mass is unchanged in a chemical reaction.

whyItMatters: Lavoisier's work on combustion is a turning point in the history of science, because it overturned the mistaken phlogiston theory and replaced it with a correct chemical understanding of burning, respiration, and rusting as combination with oxygen. In doing so he launched the chemical revolution and helped transform chemistry from a qualitative, often mystical pursuit into a rigorous quantitative science founded on careful measurement. His insistence on weighing everything, reactants and products alike including gases, established the law of conservation of mass, one of the most fundamental principles in all of chemistry, and made the balancing of chemical accounts the basis of the subject. He named oxygen and hydrogen and helped reform chemical nomenclature, giving chemistry much of its modern language, and his 1789 Elementary Treatise on Chemistry became the first modern chemistry textbook. For these achievements he is widely called the father of modern chemistry. His story also carries a lesson about credit in science, since oxygen was independently isolated by Joseph Priestley and Carl Wilhelm Scheele, and Lavoisier's genius lay in interpreting it correctly. As the work that explained combustion and founded quantitative chemistry, Lavoisier's experiments are foundational.

working.text: measure the masses of substances precisely before and after burning or heating, often in closed vessels.
observe that burning substances combine with oxygen from the air rather than releasing phlogiston, so metals gain weight.
account for all gases as well as solids to show the total mass is conserved, making chemistry quantitative.

limits: Lavoisier's contribution to understanding combustion should be described with care about credit and scope. He did not discover or first isolate oxygen; the gas was independently prepared by Carl Wilhelm Scheele around 1771 to 1772, though he published late, and by Joseph Priestley, who published first in 1775 and described it to Lavoisier, so Lavoisier's distinctive achievement was the correct interpretation and the naming of oxygen, not its isolation. His oxygen theory, though a vast improvement, was not the final word, since the modern understanding of combustion also draws on atomic theory and later chemistry that Lavoisier did not have. His idea that oxygen was the essential principle of all acids, reflected in the name he chose, later proved mistaken. Lavoisier was executed by guillotine during the French Revolution in 1794, cutting short his work. So Lavoisier's combustion work robustly established the oxygen theory and conservation of mass, understood as an interpretive triumph built partly on others' isolation of oxygen and later refined.
misreadings: Lavoisier did not discover oxygen; Scheele and Priestley isolated it first, and Lavoisier's achievement was interpreting combustion correctly and naming the gas. His oxygen theory did not spring from nowhere but replaced the phlogiston theory through careful weighing, and it was not flawless, since his belief that oxygen was in all acids proved wrong. So treating Lavoisier as the discoverer of oxygen, his theory as unaided or complete, or his every claim as correct, misreads the work that explained combustion and founded quantitative chemistry.
origin: The combustion experiments and oxygen theory of the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier in the 1770s and 1780s, culminating in his 1789 Elementary Treatise on Chemistry, which overturned phlogiston, established conservation of mass, and founded modern quantitative chemistry.
